name: Oak Park Village Hall (Council Chambers)
fact: Modernist village hall by Harry Weese, built 1975; added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2014.

name: Scoville Park
fact: Bought in 1912, it was the Park District's first parcel; the WWI 'Peace Triumphant' monument is its focal point.

name: Ridgeland Common Recreation Complex
fact: Renovated in 2014, it has a year-round regulation-size ice arena, an outdoor pool, and a dog park.

name: Rehm Park & Pool
fact: Originally called South Park; home of the free, hand-operated Rehm Park Trains.

name: Austin Gardens
fact: Nicknamed 'The Secret Garden'; about 285 trees grow on its 3.64 acres.

name: Mills Park
fact: Named for Herbert S. Mills, who bought the property in 1910; the Park District acquired it in 1939.

name: Oak Park Conservatory
fact: Greenhouse built in 1929 by Foley Greenhouse Manufacturing; on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Oak Park Public Library - Main Library
fact: The current Main Library building opened to the public on October 5, 2003.

name: Lake Street (Downtown Oak Park)
address: Lake St at Marion St, Oak Park, IL 60301
fact: Lake Street is home to both Unity Temple (875 Lake St) and the Main Library (834 Lake St).

name: Cheney Mansion
address: 220 N Euclid Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Designed in 1913 by Charles E. White Jr., a student of Frank Lloyd Wright, for the Sharpe family.

name: Taylor Park
fact: Originally North Park; renamed for Henry A. Taylor, first president of the Park Board of Commissioners.

name: Field Park
fact: Acquired in 1916 and named for children's author Eugene Field; its center was first designed by John S. Van Bergen.

name: Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio
fact: Wright built his home in 1889 and added the Studio in 1897; both are restored to their 1909 appearance.

name: Unity Temple
fact: Built 1905-08 of exposed concrete; one of eight Wright sites in a UNESCO World Heritage inscription.

name: Arthur and Grace Heurtley House
fact: Built for banker Arthur Heurtley; two colors of Roman brick are laid in alternating, projecting bands.

name: Nathan G. Moore House (Moore-Dugal House)
fact: A Tudor-style Wright design; after a 1922 fire, Wright redesigned its upper stories in 1923.

name: Frank W. Thomas House
fact: The first of Wright's mature Prairie-style residences built in Oak Park.

name: Mamah Borthwick and Edwin H. Cheney House
address: 520 N East Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: A Roman brick wall hides the raised basement, so the two-story house looks like a one-story bungalow.

name: Laura Robeson Gale House (Mrs. Thomas H. Gale House)
fact: Wright called this small stucco house with cantilevered balconies the 'progenitor of Fallingwater.'

name: Walter Gale House
fact: Among the first houses Wright designed after leaving Adler and Sullivan in 1893; note the large round turret.

name: Thomas and Laura Gale House
fact: One of the 'bootleg' houses Wright designed on his own while still working for Adler and Sullivan.

name: Peter A. Beachy House
fact: Wright's 1906 renovation of a Gothic cottage left little more than the original foundation intact.

name: George Furbeck House
address: 223 N Euclid Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Two octagonal turrets flank the entrance; designed around the same time as Wright's own Studio.

name: Oscar B. Balch House
address: 611 N Kenilworth Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Built for decorator Oscar B. Balch, whose Pebbles and Balch storefront Wright had remodeled in 1907.

name: William G. Fricke House
address: 540 Fair Oaks Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Designed during Wright's brief partnership with architect Webster Tomlinson; note the three-story tower.

name: William E. Martin House
address: 636 N East Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: William Martin's search for a home site sparked Wright's relationship with the Martin family.

name: Hills-DeCaro House
fact: Wright remodeled an 1883 house here; after a 1976 fire burned much of it, the house was rebuilt.

name: Pleasant Home (John Farson House)
fact: Prairie-style mansion by George W. Maher for banker John W. Farson; a National Historic Landmark since 1996.

name: Ernest Hemingway Birthplace
address: 339 N Oak Park Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Ernest Hemingway was born here on July 21, 1899, in his grandparents' Queen Anne house.

name: Hemingway Boyhood Home
address: 600 N Kenilworth Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Designed in 1906 for Dr. Clarence and Grace Hemingway; Ernest lived here from 1906 to 1918.

name: Scoville Square (Masonic Temple Building)
address: 119-137 N Oak Park Ave, Oak Park, IL 60301
fact: Prairie School commercial block built 1906-09 as the Masonic Temple Building; later Gilmore's Department Store.

name: Charles E. Matthews House
address: 432 N Kenilworth Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Prairie School house by Tallmadge & Watson; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2011.

name: Edward B. Kittle House
address: 636 Fair Oaks Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Prairie School house by Tallmadge & Watson; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2014.

name: Charles Schwerin House
address: 639 Fair Oaks Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Prairie School house by E.E. Roberts, built 1908; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2010.

name: Chester Flitcraft House
fact: Prairie School house (c. 1914) by John S. Van Bergen; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2010.

name: George L. Smith House
fact: Prairie School house by John S. Van Bergen, built 1915; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2012.

name: Edward and Caroline McCready House
address: 231 N Euclid Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Prairie School house by Spencer and Powers, on the same block as Wright's George Furbeck House.

name: Vernon W. Skiff House
address: 633 N East Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Prairie School house by Nimmons & Fellows, across North East Ave from Wright's William E. Martin House.

name: First Methodist Episcopal Church (First United Methodist Church)
address: 324 N Oak Park Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302
fact: Gothic Revival church by Tallmadge & Watson, built in 1923; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2005.

name: Nineteenth Century Club
fact: Neo-Classical clubhouse designed by James L. Fyfe in 1928; designated an Oak Park landmark in 2010.
